newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan reschedules $400 mln Paris Club debt.
newsitem.headline: Jordan reschedules $400 mln Paris Club debt.

text.p: Jordan has recently rescheduled $400 million owed to Paris Club creditors for up to 21-1/2 years, the finance minister said on Tuesday.

Minister of Finance, Suleiman al-Hafez, told Reuters in a written statement that the $400 million of debt were successfully rescheduled between 19.5 and 21.5 years in an accord reached last May with the Paris Club of official creditors.
On May 23 the Paris Club said it had reached agreement with Jordan on a rescheduling but gave no details.
Jordan was granted two grace periods of between 4-1/2 years and 11-1/2 years respectively, but Hafez gave no breakdown on the amounts.
The interest rates applied would be determined on a "bilateral basis," he added.
The rescheduling accord was the the fourth major and final rescheduling round, completing the restructure of $3.5-$4.0 billion debt incurred in the 1980s.
The deal would reschedule payments which were due on May 31 1997 and those due from June 1 1997 to February 28 1999, Hafez said.
Hafez said an additional $50 million would be rescheduled with non-Paris Club official creditors but he did not elaborate.
Hafez said up to 20 percent of the amounts of outstanding credit or 30 million SDR (Special Drawing Rights), whichever is higher, would be qualifed for debt conversion into investments.
Jordan's first restructuring of its debt was in 1989 after an economic crisis which forced the International Monetary Fund to intervene when the kingdom failed to service $8 billion of foreign debt.

After the disruption of the 1990 Gulf crisis, rescheduling was restarted with a February 1992 accord. The last major accord in June 1994 rescheduled $1.2 billion of the kingdom's debts over 20 years, including 10 years' grace period. A limited accord last October rescheduled debt worth a total of $308 million slated for repayment between July 1996 and May 1997.
The new accord should help Jordan reduce its debt repayment burden and cushion the impact of tough IMF-directed economic reforms. Currently Jordan pays around $500 million in debt servicing annually.

Jordan's total official debt stood at $6.4 billion of which $3.5 billion to $4 billion was owed to bilateral official creditors with the rest concessional loans from agencies such as the World Bank and Arab aid funds.
